articles.title: A Texas woman says she paid more than $130,000 for a home bought under a $47,500 contract, yet a judge ordered her to pay $45,000 in legal fees; 20 years after taking over the deal, an appeals court reversed
articles.summary: A Texas woman who says she paid more than $130,000 for a house originally bought under a $47,500 agreement has received relief from an appeals court.
articles.body: A Texas woman who says she paid more than $130,000 for a house originally bought under a $47,500 agreement has received relief from an appeals court. The court overturned an earlier ruling that required her to pay $45,000 in legal fees to the seller, finding that important questions about her payments had not been properly examined.According to Justia, the dispute involves Gloria V. Salinas, who took over a home-purchase agreement from a relative in November 2006. The original agreement, signed in 2001, required the buyer to make monthly payments towards the property. The seller, Howard A. Lang Jr., was to transfer ownership once the full amount was paid.Salinas said she had completed the payments by March 2020, more than a year before the agreement's May 2021 deadline. She claimed that she had paid more than the amount due but continued making payments because she was unsure whether the seller considered the debt settled.Lang disagreed. He maintained that Salinas had frequently paid late, owed additional charges and had not cleared the outstanding balance. The disagreement eventually led to a lawsuit in 2022, with both sides claiming that the other had failed to meet the agreement.Why the woman disputed the amount owedSalinas said the seller's records did not accurately reflect her payments. She alleged that some amounts paid towards the principal were not properly credited and that the number of remaining instalments had increased without her agreement.She also questioned the additional charges for property taxes and insurance. After comparing the seller's statements with available records, she claimed that she had been charged $1,111.88 more in property taxes and at least $1,481.88 more in insurance premiums than she owed.Late fees were another point of disagreement. Salinas calculated that she had been charged $2,977.48 in late fees over the contract period.Her payment records showed a total of $138,314.87 paid towards the agreement. She also pointed out that the seller's own statements showed that the total amount required was $136,965.74. Based on those figures, she argued that she had paid more than the amount due.Trial court orders $45,000 in legal feesSalinas approached the court in June 2022, seeking to establish that she had fulfilled her payment obligations and was entitled to the property title. Lang disputed her claims and filed a counterclaim, saying she still owed money.The case took a turn in November 2024 when the trial court considered Lang's request for summary judgment. Salinas's lawyer had withdrawn shortly before the hearing, and she appeared without legal representation.She asked the court to consider her response and supporting payment records. However, the judge granted Lang's request, citing the late filing of her response.The final order required Salinas to pay $5,401.32 in damages, along with interest and $45,000 in legal fees. The court also included additional legal fees that could apply if the matter went further on appeal.Appeals court questions seller's accountingSalinas challenged the decision, arguing that the court had not properly considered her payment records and other evidence.The Texas Fourteenth Court of Appeals found that her documents raised genuine questions about how the seller had calculated the outstanding amount. It noted that several of her claims, including uncredited principal payments and excess charges, had not been adequately addressed by the seller or his accountant.The appeals court also examined the annual payment statements that the seller was required to provide. Its review found that some statements appeared to have been sent after the January 31 deadline prescribed under Texas law.The court concluded that the available records raised enough questions about the payments and the amount allegedly owed. These issues needed further examination rather than being decided through the earlier summary judgment.In its November 24, ruling, the appeals court overturned the trial court's decision and the related $45,000 legal fee award. articles.title: Two life insurance policyholders took Transamerica to court over allegedly unpaid cash value increases; a California judge has now approved a $110 million settlement and cut lawyers’ fees to $27.5 million
articles.summary: A California federal judge has approved a $110 million settlement that ends a long-running class action lawsuit against Transamerica Life Insurance
articles.body: A California federal judge has approved a $110 million settlement that ends a long-running class action lawsuit against Transamerica Life Insurance Company. The judge also cut the legal fees requested by the policyholders' lawyers from $47.5 million to $27.5 million. The ruling settles claims brought by two policyowners, William F. Wren and John Murphy. They accused Transamerica of failing to add promised increases to the cash value of certain life insurance policies. According to Law360, in a report by Dorothy Atkins on 25 November 2026, US District Judge Jesus G. Bernal approved the $110 million settlement in the Central District of California. He also reduced the legal fees requested by the lawyers representing the class. Settlement Insight also reported that the court gave final approval to the agreement and entered judgment in late November 2026, awarding class counsel $27.5 million in fees. Under the terms published on the official settlement website, WrenCVISettlement.com, and in court filings in Wren, et al. v. Transamerica Life Insurance Company, eligible policyowners do not need to submit a claim form to receive automatic payments, provided they qualify and have not opted out.How the dispute over cash value increases startedThe lawsuit began on 1 February 2021, when Wren filed a proposed class action against Transamerica in the US District Court for the Central District of California. In April 2025, an amended complaint added Murphy as a second named plaintiff. Court records show that Wren's dispute involved a "DRL 10" second-to-die life insurance policy. Transamerica's predecessor, General Service Insurance Company, issued the policy in 1990. It covered the lives of his parents and had a face value of $1 million. These policies, known as Direct Recognition Life policies, were sold under product names or codes including Direct Recognition Life 10, Direct Recognition Life 11, DRL-10 and DRL-11. They were designed to reward policyowners who kept their coverage active for many years. Policyowners claimed that the insurance company had promised to add increases to their policies' cash value, known as CVIs, on certain anniversaries. These included the 20th, 30th and 40th years of a policy, provided premiums were paid on time.According to the amended complaint, Wren received a cash value increase of $26,889.07 on his policy's 20th anniversary in September 2010. The plaintiffs claimed that Transamerica later refused to add the promised bonuses for the 30th and 40th anniversaries. They pointed to a form letter sent in March 2016 as evidence of the company's position. They brought claims for breach of contract and, for California policyowners, breach of the duty of good faith and fair dealing. Transamerica denied the allegations. The company said it had not broken any contract, violated any law or acted improperly. Both sides eventually agreed to settle rather than continue with costly and lengthy court proceedings.Years of court battles and appealsThe lawsuit went through several stages in the federal court system before the parties reached an agreement. In November 2022, Judge Bernal granted Transamerica's request for summary judgment and closed the case. Wren appealed to the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. On 7 March 2024, the appeals court overturned the earlier decision and sent the case back to the lower court. The Ninth Circuit ruled that Wren's claims about future persistency bonuses were not blocked by claim preclusion from an earlier class action. Claim preclusion is a legal rule that can prevent someone from bringing a claim that has already been decided in an earlier case. After the case returned to the lower court, both sides continued their legal arguments before reaching an agreement through mediation. The policyowners were represented by Susman Godfrey L.L.P. and Bonnett Fairbourn Friedman & Balint, P.C. JND Legal Administration was appointed to manage the settlement.What the $110 million settlement providesAccording to the official settlement notice and court filings, the agreement creates a $110 million cash fund. The amount available to policyowners will be calculated after deductions for court-approved legal fees, expenses, payments to the named plaintiffs and administration costs. The remaining money will be shared among eligible class members. Individual payments will depend on factors including the relative value of the qualifying cash value increases connected to each policy. Settlement Insight reported that the settlement covers 2,356 Direct Recognition Life policies. Policies that have already received the full credits promised under Transamerica's crediting project will not qualify for additional payments from the fund. Other eligible policies will receive at least $100.Class counsel estimated that the average net payment could be $37,790 per class member if the court approved the full amount of legal fees originally requested. The judge's decision to reduce those fees will change the amount remaining for policyowners. The agreement also includes several commitments relating to the insurance policies. These are listed on WrenCVISettlement.com and in the court notices. The first is a bonus crediting commitment. Under this provision, Transamerica cannot cancel, withdraw or reverse certain credits that it paid or promised under its 2025 and 2026 crediting project. These include 30-year guaranteed CVIs on policies that remain active.The settlement also provides a 40-year guaranteed CVI benefit for qualifying policies that remain in force until their 40th anniversary. Another provision concerns the company's ability to challenge insurance claims. The non-contestability benefit limits Transamerica's ability to try to cancel, withdraw or deny certain death claims based on alleged problems with insurable interest or incorrect information in the original application.Fee reduction and payout timelineThe policyowners' lawyers had requested $47.5 million in legal fees. According to Law360 and Settlement Insight, this represented roughly one-third of a total value of $142.4 million that class counsel attributed to the cash settlement and other benefits. Judge Bernal reduced the requested legal fees to $27.5 million, cutting the award by $20 million. The deadlines for policyowners to opt out of the agreement or file objections passed on 2 October 2026. The court held its fairness hearing on 9 November 2026 before granting final approval. Settlement Insight reported that JND Legal Administration is expected to mail payment cheques within 60 days after the final settlement date. The agreement is due to take effect 30 days after the judgment is entered, provided no appeal is filed. Eligible policyowners who did not opt out will receive their payments automatically, without needing to submit a separate claim form.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Florida runner Casey Sparks completed seven marathons on seven continents in seven days, racing through Antarctic cold and Colombian heat; back home, he says his run has raised $20,000 to mentor boys without fathers
articles.summary: A man from Florida has completed an extraordinary endurance challenge by running seven marathons across seven continents in seven days to raise money for
articles.body: A man from Florida has completed an extraordinary endurance challenge by running seven marathons across seven continents in seven days to raise money for a nonprofit supporting boys growing up without father figures.Casey Sparks, a resident of New Smyrna Beach, took on the challenge to support No Longer Fatherless, an organisation working to connect boys in Volusia and Flagler counties with mentors who can provide guidance and support.According to WESH 2 News, Sparks covered approximately 184 miles during the week-long challenge, with a fundraising target of $100,000. He had raised around $20,000 after returning home and was hoping to generate more contributions ahead of the nonprofit's annual gala.Speaking to WESH 2 before completing the challenge, Sparks said his personal experience of losing his father had motivated him to support the cause."I lost my father when I was 18 and it's just something that kind of caught my attention," he told the news channel during a live interview from Cape Town, South Africa.He said he wanted to use the marathon challenge as an opportunity to give back and support the organisation after learning about its work through a member of his local running club.Florida runner's personal loss inspired charity challengeSparks said his connection to the cause began after meeting someone associated with No Longer Fatherless through the running club he hosts in New Smyrna Beach.The nonprofit aims to help boys without father figures in their lives by connecting them with mentors who can offer encouragement and guidance as they grow up.Sparks said the experience of losing his own father at 18 made the organisation's mission particularly meaningful to him.He decided to dedicate his seven-continent running challenge to the nonprofit and raise funds for its work.The runner also described the journey as a major personal milestone, revealing that it was the first time he had travelled outside the United States.Antarctica was toughest marathon, Colombia his favouriteAfter returning to Florida, Sparks spoke to WESH 2 anchor Michelle Imperato about his experience, describing the challenge as an extraordinary journey.He said the marathon in Cartagena, Colombia, was his favourite of the seven races, particularly because he managed to win the sixth event despite the hot and humid conditions.Antarctica, however, proved to be the toughest stop.Sparks said temperatures dropped to around minus 23 degrees Celsius, with additional wind chill making the conditions even more difficult."Being from Florida, it was so cold," he told WESH 2, describing how his gloves froze in place and ice formed around his eyes during the race.Despite the difficult conditions, Sparks completed the seven-marathon challenge and returned home over the weekend.He said he hoped to make another fundraising push to move closer to his $100,000 target.The nonprofit's work focuses on helping boys in Volusia and Flagler counties find positive male mentors, with the aim of ensuring that children growing up without fathers have someone they can turn to for support.You use AI every articles.title: A Mississippi woman lost her husband just seven months after their wedding; a court has upheld her right to the remaining proceeds of his house sale but ruled his separately held retirement funds belong to his estate
articles.summary: A Mississippi appeals court has ruled that a widow cannot keep her late husband's retirement savings despite receiving the money from the account
articles.body: A Mississippi appeals court has ruled that a widow cannot keep her late husband's retirement savings despite receiving the money from the account administrator after his death, citing a prenuptial agreement that kept the couple's assets separate.The Mississippi Court of Appeals upheld a lower court's decision that Robert D McLean's 401(k) retirement account belonged to his estate rather than his wife, Jennifer Feazell McLean. The ruling, delivered on November 24, 2026, followed a legal dispute involving the validity of their prenuptial agreement and the ownership of assets after Robert's unexpected death.The couple had married in May 2021 after dating for around six years and living together for three years. They signed a prenuptial agreement four days before their wedding, agreeing that their individual properties and financial assets would remain separate.Robert died unexpectedly in January 2022, around seven months after the marriage. His 401(k), which had a balance of approximately $319,516, was subsequently transferred to Jennifer by the account administrator in her capacity as his surviving spouse.However, Robert's son, Bailey McLean, and his father's estate challenged her ownership of the money, seeking to enforce the prenuptial agreement.Wife challenged prenup, argued husband did not disclose all assetsJennifer challenged the validity of the agreement, arguing that Robert had not fully disclosed his financial assets before their marriage.She pointed to several assets that were allegedly missing from the agreement, including a property worth approximately $35,000, a Central Bank account, an interest in a pension fund and a second boat.The estate argued that Robert had disclosed assets worth at least $500,000 and that Jennifer had sufficient knowledge of his financial circumstances after their six-year relationship and three years of living together.The agreement also recorded Jennifer's acknowledgement that Robert had provided a full and fair disclosure of his assets, liabilities, income and financial worth.The appeals court agreed with the lower court that the prenuptial agreement was valid and enforceable. It said the financial disclosures, the couple's representations in the agreement and Jennifer's knowledge of Robert's financial circumstances supported the conclusion that she had a reasonable understanding of his financial position.The court also noted that Jennifer had been informed of her right to seek independent legal advice but had chosen not to hire her own attorney.Why court awarded 401(k) to husband's estateA key issue in the dispute was that the retirement account administrator had already transferred the money to Jennifer after Robert's death.The court explained that under the federal Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA), a surviving spouse is generally entitled to certain retirement benefits unless the spouse has provided the required written consent to waive them.Robert's prenuptial agreement did not meet the strict requirements for an ERISA spousal waiver. Therefore, the account administrator had acted properly in transferring the retirement money to Jennifer.However, the court said that the payment did not prevent Robert's son and estate from subsequently pursuing a separate legal claim under the prenuptial agreement.It upheld the lower court's finding that the retirement savings were Robert's separate property and belonged to his estate. By retaining the funds after receiving them, Jennifer had breached the terms of the agreement, the court ruled.The appeals court also upheld an award of $9,838.04 in legal fees to Robert's son and estate. The prenuptial agreement required a party challenging its validity to pay the other side's legal expenses if the challenge was unsuccessful.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: A metal detectorist in England found little for months before unearthing a rare 380-year-old square coin in an Essex field; the British Museum is set to examine it, and he may not get to keep it
articles.summary: A British metal detectorist has finally found something valuable after months of digging up scrap metal.
articles.body: A British metal detectorist has finally found something valuable after months of digging up scrap metal. His latest discovery is a rare, 380-year-old square silver coin found in a farmer's field in Essex. The finder, who has chosen to remain anonymous, had been searching the same area near Braintree for several months without much success. He was close to giving up that day when his metal detector signalled something buried about six inches below the ground.The unique 1646 Siege PieceThe object he uncovered was very different from an ordinary English coin. It is a square piece of hammered silver measuring about 2.5cm (one inch) across. The coin carries the date "1646" and the initials "CR", which stand for King Charles I. It also has the inscription "CAROLVS D G MAG BRIT FRAN ET HIB REX". This translates as "Charles, by the Grace of God, King of Great Britain, France and Ireland." A crown and the value "II S", meaning two shillings, also appear on the coin. These details identify it as a rare "siege piece", also known as "notgeld", a form of emergency money made during times of crisis.Historical context of the Civil War coinThe coin was made during the English Civil War, which lasted from 1642 to 1651. The conflict was fought between supporters of King Charles I, known as Royalists or Cavaliers, and Parliament's supporters, known as Parliamentarians or Roundheads. The Parliamentarians were led by figures including Oliver Cromwell. As the war continued, Parliament took control of London and the Royal Mint. Royalist towns and strongholds that came under siege then began making their own coins. They needed money to pay soldiers and keep trade going inside their walls. These siege coins were often made quickly and with little care. Because silver and other materials were in short supply, makers sometimes used silver plates or other scrap metal. The square shape may have made production easier, as it needed less cutting and preparation than a round coin. The "II S" marking suggests that the coin may have been made at a Royalist mint in Carlisle or Newark.Independent research and data challengesAfter finding the coin, the detectorist began looking into its history and possible value. Its age and rarity quickly showed that it was an important discovery. Other Civil War siege coins have been sold at auctions, with some reaching high prices because so few examples exist. However, finding an accurate estimate for this particular 1646 square coin is difficult. There is a small market for rare coins of this kind, and they do not come up for sale often. Their prices can also vary widely depending on their condition, history of ownership and the auction house handling the sale. Despite the difficulty in estimating its value, the coin is clearly a major find for the detectorist.British Museum examination and the Portable Antiquities SchemeThe finder reported the discovery to the local Finds Liaison Officer (FLO) in Essex, following the legal reporting process. The role is part of the Portable Antiquities Scheme (PAS), a programme run by the British Museum and Amgueddfa Cymru, Museum Wales. The scheme records archaeological objects found by members of the public. These discoveries help researchers learn more about Britain's history. The local officer quickly recognised that the coin could be important. Because it may qualify as Treasure, it has been sent to the British Museum in London. Expert curators will examine it and confirm its identity and status.The legal implications of Treasure and ownershipThe finder may not be able to keep the coin, depending on the outcome of the examination. Its ownership will be decided under the Treasure Act 1996. Under the Act, an object found in England, Wales or Northern Ireland can be classed as Treasure if it is more than 300 years old and contains at least 10 per cent precious metal, such as gold or silver. Objects that meet the legal conditions belong to the Crown. Although the finder may not be allowed to keep the coin, the law provides for compensation. If the British Museum decides to add it to its national collection, an independent group called the Treasure Valuation Committee will assess its market value. The museum will then pay the finder a reward based on that valuation. The landowner whose field produced the coin is also usually entitled to a share of the reward. If the British Museum and other accredited museums decide not to acquire it, the coin may be disclaimed and returned to the finder. The British Museum's experts will make the final decision on the coin's status and value. The detectorist from Essex is now waiting to learn what will happen to his discovery.You use AI every day. articles.title: Road ministry tightens bidding norms to keep poor performers out of fully govt-funded projects
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The road transport ministry has linked contractors’ bidding capacity to their performance ratings and delays in ongoing projects, replacing the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The road transport ministry has linked contractors’ bidding capacity to their performance ratings and delays in ongoing projects, replacing the earlier practice of assessing their best-performing financial year for fully government-funded or EPC projects.These changes in the bidding and contract conditions have been made to address concerns over the quality of construction and delays in project execution. The modifications in the Request for Proposal (RFP) for Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) contracts, which replaced the existing framework issued in March 2019, seek to make the contractor selection process more performance-oriented. This will prevent contractors with a poor execution record from taking on additional projects beyond their capacity.The revised framework also does away with sequential counter-offers to the second and third lowest bidders. If the lowest bidder is found ineligible, the authority can annul the bidding process and invite fresh bids.Further, the ministry has brought in stricter norms for joint ventures (JVs), reducing the maximum number of members from three to two. JVs will generally be allowed only for projects costing more than Rs 1,000 crore, with enhanced minimum participation requirements for the other member.Technical eligibility conditions have also been strengthened, particularly for major bridges, structures and tunnels, to ensure that contractors bidding for specialised infrastructure projects have relevant experience.The modified RFP links performance security to contractors’ ratings, with the requirement ranging from 3% to 5% of the bid price. It also provides for electronic submission of security instruments.Further, the ministry has rationalised the number of non-performance criteria from 20 to seven, with clearly defined thresholds and assessment periods. Provisions dealing with catastrophic failures, termination of projects, debarment and insolvency have also been strengthened.To improve transparency, bidders will have to disclose details of ongoing disputes, litigation, arbitration and penal actions and keep such information updated during the bidding process.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Sheshnag Lake row: Karan Singh questions need for wider road, PDP steps up heat
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: The controversy over the presence of heavy machinery near the ecologically fragile Sheshnag Lake along the Amarnath Yatra route shows no signs
articles.body: SRINAGAR: The controversy over the presence of heavy machinery near the ecologically fragile Sheshnag Lake along the Amarnath Yatra route shows no signs of dying down, with former Sadr-i-Riyasat (head of state) of Jammu & Kashmir, Karan Singh, saying every pilgrimage route need not be turned into a multi-lane road for the convenience of tourists. Mehbooba Mufti-led PDP has also stepped up its campaign, demanding that govt allow a joint team of politicians and environmentalists to visit the lake and make the site accessible for an independent assessment.Joining the voices opposing the move, Karan Singh, in a social media post, said: “We do not have to make every pilgrim route into a motorable road just for the convenience of tourists. Genuine pilgrims will not mind walking or riding towards this great shrine.”Mehbooba demanded transparency in the matter, saying if no work was taking place near the lake, as assured by forest minister Altaf Kaloo, there was no reason to prevent people from visiting the site.“How did JCBs reach Sheshnag? Who authorised their movement, and what action has been taken against those responsible?” she asked at a press conference.Mehbooba said chief minister Omar Abdullah had signed a memorandum of understanding with the Border Roads Organisation (BRO) in Jan, assigning it the work of constructing a track in the area. She demanded that the agreement be made public and asked why people were not being allowed to travel from Pahalgam to Chandanwari and beyond.J&K government on Wednesday dismissed allegations of construction near the high-altitude lake, with Kaloo saying the JCB machinery was operating 200-300 feet away and at a higher elevation.As an online petition demanding an immediate halt to excavation and road-widening work near the lake crossed over 16,000 signatures Thursday, environmental activist Raja Muzaffar Bhat said he received a “distressing SOS” last night from a young nature lover, Zarqua Banday, who was allegedly being harassed for starting the petition. Bhat said cyber police had called her family.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Marble slab taken from Taj Mahal by East India Company officer to go under hammer in London
articles.summary: TOI Correspondent from London: A marble slab from the Taj Mahal taken by a senior East India Company officer during the British Raj, which stayed in his
articles.body: TOI Correspondent from London: A marble slab from the Taj Mahal taken by a senior East India Company officer during the British Raj, which stayed in his English family for over 200 years, will be put up for auction in the UK on Dec 9.Colonel Pownoll Phipps (1780-1858), the British superintendent of historic buildings in Agra, who was in charge of repairs of the Taj Mahal and other historic buildings, found the marble slab in an underground room beneath the Taj Mahal and thought it was intended for the repair work. He was permitted to keep it, according to his son’s memoirs.It is one of two marble panels Phipps collected from the Taj Mahal in 1816 at the end of his tenure in Agra. During that time, he was once sent to the Taj Mahal to prevent an Englishwoman from picking agates out of the marble with a steel fork.Cut as a rectangle with chamfered corners, the slab is carved and inlaid with polished and flattened agate, jasper, chalcedony and other semi-precious stones.The floral border around the slab is the same as the border around the edge of the upper flat surface of the cenotaph of Shah Jahan in the Taj Mahal, and the floral scroll is similar to the left-hand scroll on top of the cenotaph.The 55.8cm x 45.2cm x 3cm slab will go under the hammer at Lyon & Turnbull auctioneers in London and online as a highlight of the Islamic and Indian Art sale. It is estimated to sell for £20,000 to £30,000 (Rs 24 lakh to Rs 36 lakh).Kristina Sanne, head of the Lyon & Turnbull Islamic and Indian Art department, said: “It is a privilege to offer a piece with such a comprehensive history and that is linked to one of the most famous buildings in the world. The fact that it has turned up 210 years after being brought home by a senior British functionary, and still in his family, is quite extraordinary.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Restorers working inside England's centuries-old Tamworth Castle found a 1960s cigarette packet, an old newspaper and pieces of a tea chest hidden in ceilings and skirting during a £1.9 million conservation project
articles.summary: A forgotten cigarette packet, a newspaper frozen in time and fragments of an old tea chest are offering an unexpected glimpse into everyday life at one of
articles.body: A forgotten cigarette packet, a newspaper frozen in time and fragments of an old tea chest are offering an unexpected glimpse into everyday life at one of England’s historic castles. Hidden for decades behind ceilings and skirting boards, the ordinary objects are emerging as specialist restorers peel back layers of alterations at Tamworth Castle, revealing stories left behind by generations of people who lived and worked there.According to Tamworth Borough Council, the discoveries were made during a £1.9 million conservation programme, the largest restoration project in the castle’s modern history. Now entering its second phase, the work focuses on the South Wing as contractors address essential repairs while documenting the building’s hidden history.Everyday objects become historical cluesAmong the latest discoveries is a pale green Woodbine cigarette packet found above a ceiling on the southern side of the castle. Believed to date from the 1950s or early 1960s, the packaging retains part of its original foil lining and carries the manufacturer's branding and the slogan 'Wills for Quality'.Tamworth Borough Council notes that Woodbine was introduced in 1888 and became a familiar name in British social history, particularly during the first half of the 20th century. The packet's location suggests a tradesperson may have accidentally left it behind during an earlier repair or renovation.Another find emerged from behind the skirting board in Cooke's Bedroom. It was part of the Daily Express dated Wednesday, November 27, 1968. The newspaper's headline, 'Later to School', alongside reports about cigarette manufacturers and pricing, offers a snapshot of British life nearly six decades ago.In the Georgian Room, restorers also uncovered timber fragments from what appears to have been an old tea chest. Reused within the ceiling structure, the pieces still carry traces of stencilled lettering, including the words 'Paris' and 'Grand'. According to the council, the discovery demonstrates how materials were repurposed rather than discarded during earlier building work.A much older history beneath the surfacesThese recent finds add to a growing collection of discoveries made during the restoration. In September 2026, contractors working in the Townshend Room gift shop uncovered an intact lead-lined sink concealed inside a deep windowsill.Tamworth Borough Council believes the feature dates from the 18th or 19th century and indicates that the room may once have served as a pantry or domestic service area. Its lead lining was shaped over a wooden structure, with drainage holes individually punched into the metal. The sink will be protected and concealed again as the room is reinstated.Earlier archaeological investigations beneath the modern kitchen area also revealed medieval pottery and animal bones. The ceramic fragments, believed to date from the 13th to 15th centuries, include green-glazed pottery and cooking vessel remains. Cattle, sheep, and game bird bones with butchery marks reveal the castle's former residents' diet.A sheep toe bone with a drilled hole was particularly intriguing, as it may have been reused as a toggle.Meanwhile, removing sections of ornate panelling in the Oak Room exposed a mysterious carving of three arrows inside a shield. Its purpose remains uncertain, with possibilities ranging from a craftsman's mark to a decorative or heraldic symbol.Preserving a thousand years of historyThe conservation programme is supported by £1,716,238 from Arts Council England's Museum Estate and Development Fund (MEND), alongside £190,695 from Tamworth Borough Council.According to the council, future work will include stabilising the North Wing's bay windows, walls and historic openings, alongside essential repairs to the motte and surrounding slopes.Dating back almost 1,000 years, Tamworth Castle has evolved from an Anglo-Saxon centre of power into a Norman fortress, medieval stronghold, historic residence and public museum.Tamworth Borough Council's Caring for the Castle programme aims to safeguard the nationally significant building for future generations while allowing visitors to experience its continuing conservation journey.Although scaffolding, temporary closures and changing access arrangements are expected, the council is keeping the castle open wherever possible. As restoration progresses, the discoveries demonstrate that preserving a historic building is not simply about repairing its walls, but also uncovering the everyday lives embedded within them.Images Courtesy: Tamworth Borough CouncilYou use AI every day. articles.title: Kai Cenat launches separate YouTube gaming channel after completing GTA VI, but Mizkif calls it ‘forced’
articles.summary: Kai Cenat has launched a separate YouTube gaming channel, but not everyone is convinced about his latest move.
articles.body: Kai Cenat has launched a separate YouTube gaming channel, but not everyone is convinced about his latest move. The Twitch star introduced @KaiCenatGaming on November 25, 2026, with a video titled Welcome To My Gaming Channel.... He explained that the channel would feature offline gameplay, horror games and different types of games. He also asked viewers to suggest what they want to watch. However, fellow streamer Mizkif questioned the move and claimed that Kai was forcing himself into gaming content.Kai Cenat explains what viewers can expect from his new YouTube gaming channelIn his first video, Kai Cenat explained that he wanted a separate place to share more gaming content without having to make every session a livestream. He said:"Welcome to my gaming channel where we'll be doing a whole bunch of offline gaming, horror games, fun games, every type of game. All right. Um, I got a lot of fun stuff lined up for us, and I cannot wait, but I got to keep everything a secret, and I got to make sure that we stay consistent."The 24-year-old streamer also made it clear that he has several ideas ready for the channel. However, he did not reveal which games he plans to play first. Instead, he asked viewers to share their suggestions in the comments.He also wants to make sure the channel stays active. Regular uploads will be important if he wants viewers to keep coming back after subscribing.Kai further explained that he sometimes wants to enjoy games without having to stream the entire experience. He said:"Please do me a favor and comment what games y'all would like to see. I really hope I'm very consistent on this channel, but I'm also excited because there will be some times where I just want to game and just dive deeper into that. So, this is what this channel is for. So, hopefully you guys are ready, and I can't wait to see you guys soon. Later. Goodbye."His recent gaming activity gives some idea of why he wants to explore this format. Kai spent more than 130 hours playing five GTA titles, including GTA III, Vice City, San Andreas, GTA IV and GTA V. He completed the games before moving on to GTA VI.He then spent around 67 hours on his GTA VI livestream before completing the story on November 21. The long sessions showed how much time he was willing to spend on gaming content. His new channel will give him another way to share that interest with viewers.Mizkif questions Kai Cenat's decision to start a separate gaming channelNot everyone was impressed by Kai Cenat's announcement. Kick streamer Mizkif shared his reaction and suggested that Kai was not genuinely interested in making gaming content."I'll be real with Kai. When it comes to gaming and that kinda content... He doesn't like that kinda content. It's very obvious that this is all so forced and fake. So, no one cares," Mizkif said.He also questioned whether gaming content would suit Kai's existing audience. According to Mizkif, most of Kai's viewers are not particularly interested in watching traditional gaming videos.He explained his point further:"I mean, like, his audience is kinda normie as ****. You don't like video games like that; you don't need a gaming channel, so why are you doing this? You know? I feel like someone like him, who really wants to push and become the next big thing, is gonna go into gaming and just do that route? I don't know."Mizkif's comments raise a question about whether Kai's existing viewers will follow him to a channel focused mainly on recorded gameplay. However, Kai has already made his plans clear. He wants to try different games and give himself more time to enjoy them away from live broadcasts.For now, the channel is in its early days, and Kai has yet to reveal his first full gaming upload.Gaming is not a completely new direction for Kai. articles.title: A federal appeals court gives Donald Trump a new route to challenge his 34-count New York criminal conviction, sending the case back to a judge and putting his separate state appeal on hold
articles.summary: Donald Trump’s long-running legal battle over his historic criminal conviction has entered another unexpected turn, giving the US president a fresh
articles.body: Donald Trump’s long-running legal battle over his historic criminal conviction has entered another unexpected turn, giving the US president a fresh opportunity to challenge a verdict that once made him the first former or sitting American president convicted of a crime. A federal appeals court has reopened the possibility of moving the case out of New York state jurisdiction, potentially creating a new legal route through which Trump could seek to have his conviction overturned on presidential immunity grounds. The decision marks a significant development in a case that has continued to generate legal and political consequences, despite the original trial concluding more than a year ago.Appeals court reopens the federal routeAccording to AP News, a three-judge panel of the 2nd US Circuit Court of Appeals has sent the matter back to a federal district court, directing a judge to promptly reconsider Trump's request to transfer his New York hush-money case from state to federal jurisdiction.The decision reverses an earlier position taken by the late federal judge Alvin Hellerstein, who had repeatedly rejected Trump's attempts to move the proceedings. Hellerstein, who died in October at the age of 92, had most recently denied the request in August.The appeals court's intervention does not automatically transfer the case or overturn the conviction. Instead, it gives Trump's legal team another opportunity to establish that the proceedings should have been handled in federal court.As The Guardian reported, a favourable decision at the district court level could allow Trump to return to the appeals court and pursue arguments that the conviction should be dismissed under presidential immunity protections.The conviction at the centre of the disputeThe case originated from a $130,000 payment made by Trump's former lawyer Michael Cohen to adult-film performer Stormy Daniels ahead of the 2016 presidential election. Daniels had alleged a sexual encounter with Trump, which he denies.Prosecutors argued that Trump subsequently reimbursed Cohen through a series of payments falsely recorded as legal expenses, concealing the original transaction and helping protect his election campaign from potentially damaging publicity. In May 2024, a Manhattan jury found Trump guilty on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records. He received no punishment in the case.The president has consistently denied wrongdoing and has pursued multiple legal challenges in an effort to overturn the verdict.Argument hinges on presidential immunityAccording to The Independent, Trump's lawyers have argued that prosecutors relied on evidence involving White House activities, conversations with aides and social media posts that should have been protected under the Supreme Court's decision.His legal team has also challenged the prosecution's interpretation of the hush-money payment as an unlawful campaign finance contribution, arguing that aspects of the case involve federal rather than state law.However, Manhattan prosecutors have maintained that the conduct underlying the conviction concerned private actions and state-level offences rather than Trump's official presidential responsibilities.Hellerstein had previously rejected the immunity argument, reasoning that paying hush money to an adult-film performer and concealing an embarrassing episode did not fall within the protection afforded to presidential duties.State appeal faces an uncertain futureThe federal court development could also disrupt Trump's parallel attempt to overturn the conviction through New York's state appellate system.AP News reported that the state appeal had already progressed to arguments before the Appellate Division earlier in November, with a decision still pending.Following the federal appeals court's latest order, Trump's lawyers asked the state court to pause further proceedings while questions surrounding federal jurisdiction are resolved.In a complicated procedural process, the case may bounce between federal courts before Trump's immunity arguments are heard again, according to The Guardian.What happens next?The immediate responsibility now rests with the federal district court, which must reconsider whether the case qualifies for transfer from state jurisdiction. The outcome may determine whether Trump can appeal his federal immunity conviction. However, even a favourable ruling would not automatically erase the jury's verdict.Trump's appeals court win is procedural, not criminal. His efforts to overturn the 34-count conviction remain ongoing, leaving the future of the historic New York prosecution dependent on another round of judicial scrutiny.Image Courtesy: InstagramYou use AI every day. articles.title: Kansas man cleaning out a shed in Girard finds rusty metal box frozen shut; inside was his father-in-law's 1945 letter describing Japan's World War II surrender in Tokyo Bay
articles.summary: A Kansas man cleaning out a shed in Girard has found a rusty metal box frozen shut, and inside was a World War II letter his late father-in-law wrote home
articles.body: A Kansas man cleaning out a shed in Girard has found a rusty metal box frozen shut, and inside was a World War II letter his late father-in-law wrote home in 1945 after watching Japan sign its surrender in Tokyo Bay. Dan Curry found the box after his brother-in-law died. The letter, from Navy radioman Don Lamb, was addressed to his parents and gave a firsthand account of a turning point in world history. Curry's wife discovered the letter as she sorted through everything inside, and reading it brought the whole family closer to a loved one they had lost.How a rusty metal box frozen shut in a Girard shed revealed a Navy radioman's 1945 letterAccording to Four States, Curry's first instinct was to toss the dirty old box outside, though he could tell something was inside. He took it home and forced it open. His wife began crying as she read the letter, which turned out to be from her father, Don Lamb of Girard.What Navy radioman Don Lamb told his parents as his ship sailed into Tokyo Bay in September 1945Lamb served aboard the USS Mount Olympus. The first page greets his parents, asks after Hellen and describes rough seas as the ship nears Tokyo Bay, promising more news the next day. Page two opens with Lamb saying he was back, that the war seemed to be over and that the peace treaty had been signed, with the crew getting to watch.Why 2 September 1945 mattered, as Japan signed its Instrument of Surrender in Tokyo BayThe letter dates to the day the Japanese signed the Instrument of Surrender aboard the USS Missouri. The Mount Olympus was one of more than 300 American warships escorting the battleship. Lamb's captain was aboard the Missouri for the ceremony, and Curry said Lamb watched events unfold from the upper part of his own ship.The ceremony followed weeks of momentous events. Tokyo Bay became a safe harbour for Allied ships after the Japanese emperor agreed to surrender on 15 August 1945, following the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, according to the US Department of Energy.The Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum reports that fighting continued in places where Japanese commands had not received, or did not believe, news of the surrender. Because of fears that kamikaze pilots might try to disrupt the ceremony, the Navy kept the remaining ships of its fast carrier force offshore, ready to provide fighter cover. Moments after the ceremony ended, 349 carrier aircraft flew overhead in a massed formation, though some sources put the figure at 450.A closing request to keep the envelope: How Don Lamb's message reached his family 81 years laterLamb ended the letter by asking his parents to keep the envelope, since someone might want to see it one day. Curry told Four States Homepage that reading it felt as though Lamb were sitting in front of the family, speaking to them. His advice to others is simple, "Don't throw away old things until you look at them."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Special Parliament session from November 30; women’s quota on agenda
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Ending suspense, government Thursday moved to convene a short session of Parliament from November 30 during which it is expected to bring back
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Ending suspense, government Thursday moved to convene a short session of Parliament from November 30 during which it is expected to bring back the delimitation bills to implement the women’s quota law from 2029, which would increase Lok Sabha’s maximum strength to 850 from 550, reflecting confidence in NDA that it will muster a two-thirds majority this time to secure the bill’s passage.Parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju announced that government has requested Speaker Om Birla to reconvene Lok Sabha on November 30 and Rajya Sabha Chairman C P Radhakrishnan to call a sitting of the House on Dec 2 to transact “essential government business”.“Subject to exigencies of business, the sitting of both Houses may conclude on Dec 3, 2026,” he said, suggesting government is hopeful of concluding its agenda in four days.This is the second attempt by government to secure passage of its ambitious legislative agenda. If passed, it will mark the biggest realignment of Lok Sabha constituencies since Independence. A united opposition had thwarted the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill in a similarly convened session, of three days, from April 16.The move comes amid strong indications that government is confident of its numbers in the second trial of strength that the opposition is determined to force. In any case, it will be loath to risk another embarrassment; that too one during the build-up to assembly elections in UP and other states.Passage of the bill, which will ensure reservation of one-third seats in Lok Sabha and pave the way for a similar quota in assemblies, will give BJP a major campaign point in the upcoming polls to showcase its pro-women credentials.Shah’s assurance may be added to delimitation bill, Cabinet nod todayIn an article on Thursday, PM Narendra Modi said the scuttling of the bill earlier this year “should fill our hearts with shame”, adding that a legislation aimed at giving adequate representation to women was prevented from being passed by one opposition party, in what was an attack at Congress.He assured women that “no force can prevent us from ensuring that justice is done to them.”Last time, among 528 MPs present in Lok Sabha, the bill had received support from 298 members while 230 opposed it, falling way short of the 352 needed for its passage.Smarting under the government’s first defeat on the floor of Parliament, BJP has since made determined moves to shore up its numbers, helped considerably by fractures in the opposition camp.The switchover of 20 of 29 Trinamool Congress Lok Sabha MPs to NDA has boosted its numbers. Going by the buzz within government, it is also counting on support of 22 DMK MPs and eight of NCP-SP, who had voted against the bill last time along with TMC’s entire lot.Lok Sabha’s current strength is 540, with NDA’s tally at 321. The support of DMK and NCP-SP will take it to 351. The expected support from four YSR Congress MPs will take it closer to the 360-mark required in case all 540 MPs vote, which is unlikely as a few abstentions are expected to NDA’s advantage.Government has maintained secrecy about its potential new backers. DMK and NCP-SP have not announced support but have suggested that they can back the bill if states are not discriminated against — a threshold that government can easily meet by writing into the bill, which is already in Parliament, a clause providing for 50 per cent increase in seats across the board.Union minister Amit Shah had assured Lok Sabha in April that no state would suffer erosion in its relative strength in the lower House as the number of seats in each state would rise by around 50 per cent. The strength of state assemblies will be next to go up if the bill is passed. Shah’s assurance may be pencilled into the bill, which the Union cabinet headed by PM Narendra Modi is likely to clear Friday.A DMK MP told TOI that party chief MK Stalin will finalise their stand after looking at the bill, reiterating that southern states should not suffer. DMK has anyway drifted away from the opposition after Congress dumped it to align with CM Vijay-led TVK in Tamil Nadu.NCP MP Supriya Sule said “let the bill be out first”, suggesting her openness to the proposal. She said the bill may be good and needed to be studied first, and that opposition and government had in the past supported decisions which were in national interest.The hard part for the government is in the Lok Sabha, as its numbers are more favourably aligned in the Rajya Sabha.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Health insurer refused to pay for 9-year-old’s $27,000 ear surgery, calling it cosmetic; how his parents overturned the denial through external review as 52% of New York appeals succeeded
articles.summary: A Brooklyn family’s fight with health insurer Aetna has drawn attention to how patients can challenge denied medical claims.
articles.body: A Brooklyn family’s fight with health insurer Aetna has drawn attention to how patients can challenge denied medical claims. After the company classified their 9-year-old son’s $27,000 ear surgery as “cosmetic”, despite his doctors describing it as medically necessary, his parents took the case to an independent external review, and won.Nadine Friedman and Jared Roberts had watched their son, Ozzie Roberts, deal with Goldenhar Syndrome, a rare condition that, according to his medical records, caused pain, redness and growth problems in his right ear.“A lot of nights during the week, just midway through the night, [he was] just crying, screaming. It was really tough to see,” Roberts said.In February, doctors performed an ear-pinning surgery on Ozzie, which helped address the problem. However, the family then faced a months-long dispute over the cost of the procedure after Aetna refused to cover it.Why Aetna denied the $27,000 surgeryAetna classified the procedure as cosmetic, even though Ozzie’s doctors had stated that it was medically necessary. His parents first appealed directly to the insurer, but their request was unsuccessful.“I would absolutely never do anything like this unless it absolutely impeded on his health and his life,” Friedman said.Aetna said the doctor’s “original submitted billing code is typically for coverage of a cosmetic procedure and warranted further review.” The company also acknowledged how challenging a healthcare episode can be for families, but declined to be interviewed by CBS News New York.How the parents overturned the insurance denialAfter the initial appeal failed, the family sought an external review. In New York, state-appointed independent organisations can examine insurance denials and decide whether they should be reversed.Earlier this fall, the family learned that the external appeal had succeeded and Aetna would cover the surgery.Friedman said the process required considerable time and effort, something not every family may be able to manage.“Which is great, but it's only because I have a flexible job, time to document these things,” she said. “I'm really pushy, I'm fighting these things, and in the end, you have to become, like, a part-time insurance lawyer, basically, to do these things.”Despite securing coverage, the experience has prompted Friedman to push for broader changes. She is supporting the Ensuring Lasting Smiles Act, a proposed federal bill that would require insurers to cover necessary treatments for people with congenital anomalies or birth defects.More than half of New York’s external appeals overturnedThe family’s experience comes amid wider questions about how often insurance denials are reversed when patients challenge them.Researchers Ayesha Rahim of Brown University and Joseph Dov Bruch of Weill Cornell have studied the outcomes of external appeals. They found that 52% of denials that reached external review in New York State last year were overturned.“We did find that a majority of external appeals are overturned,” Rahim said.Bruch said reversals could happen for several reasons, including human or technological errors, ambiguity in insurance policies or potentially inappropriate conduct by insurers.What insurers say about denied claimsCBS News New York also sought a response from the New York Health Plan Association, a nonprofit trade association representing around 20 major insurers in the state.Its CEO, Eric Linzer, said the vast majority of requested services are provided. However, he argued that a doctor’s assessment of medical necessity is not the only factor insurers consider when reviewing a claim.“Oftentimes, you wanna make sure that the services being requested abide by peer-reviewed evidence, specialty society guidelines,” Linzer said. He also noted that there can be significant variation among providers.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Seven months of mediation proceedings, which were conducted on the direction of the SC for amicable resolution of the property dispute between late industrialist Sunjay Kapur’s mother, Rani Kapur, and his widow, Priya Sachdev Kapur, fell flat, and the former CJI DY Chandrachud, who was the mediator, told the court Thursday that the mediation reached an impasse despite 15 sittings.He was roped in by the SC in May to settle the high-profile property dispute between them over Kapur’s Rs 30,000 crore estate.Taking note of the report filed by the mediator, a bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran closed the mediation. “One can never force a settlement,” it observed.As the lawyers appearing for the Kapurs blamed each other’s clients for mediation failure, the bench told the parties, “When you all decide to sit, talk, and try to find a way out, you need to show some flexibility, some understanding, and take a practical view of the matter... 15 sittings and you all couldn’t reach a conclusion.”The court said that it would pass a short order in the case.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: South African father and son duo built a drone that reached 510 km/h after their first model missed out on a world record, using a new carbon-fibre design and months of testing to achieve Guinness World Records recognition
articles.summary: A drone capable of travelling faster than 480 km/h is the result of months of design work, repeated testing and engineering adjustments by a father and
articles.body: A drone capable of travelling faster than 480 km/h is the result of months of design work, repeated testing and engineering adjustments by a father and son in South Africa. Luke Bell and his father Mike developed a battery-powered quadcopter called Peregreen 2, which set a Guinness World Records title in 2024 for the fastest ground speed by a battery-powered remote-controlled quadcopter. Its officially recognised average speed was 480.23 km/h (298.47 mph), although the aircraft reached a peak measured speed of 510 km/h (317 mph) during the record attempts. The pair faced overheating components, electrical fires and several failed tests before the drone was ready for its official runs.How a father-son duo from South Africa created the world's fastest battery-powered droneThe project was based in South Africa's Western Cape, where Luke and Mike spent several months working on the quadcopter. Peregreen 2 was not their first attempt at building a high-speed drone. An earlier version, named Peregreen, had reached 397 km/h (247 mph), but that performance did not result in an officially recognised Guinness World Records title.The father-and-son team returned to the design with changes intended to improve its speed and flight performance. The development process involved more than simply fitting powerful motors. The shape, weight distribution and overall construction of the aircraft all needed attention, particularly because a quadcopter travelling at such speeds faces considerable aerodynamic resistance.Their revised machine eventually achieved an officially recorded average ground speed of 480.23 km/h. During the two record-setting runs, its onboard measurements also registered a maximum speed of 510 km/h (317 mph). At that pace, the drone can cover approximately 142 metres in a second, as reported by Guinness World Records.Technical setbacks to build a high-speed droneGetting Peregreen 2 into the air at high speed involved a number of technical setbacks. During testing, some of its electrical components struggled to cope with the demands placed on them. Wires and batteries became so hot that they caused electrical fires, forcing the team to address problems with the design before continuing.Its outer shell was made from carbon fibre, a lightweight material that helped keep the drone's weight down. The team also developed a redesigned shape that was 3D-printed at a workshop before being fitted with motors, batteries and other components. The new design was intended to improve aerodynamic performance, an important consideration for a quadcopter travelling at extremely high speeds.The body was reshaped to make it more aerodynamic. This mattered because air resistance becomes an increasingly significant obstacle as an aircraft accelerates. The Bells also received guidance from aerothermal engineer Chris Rosser, who helped them work through the challenges involved in controlling a quadcopter at such high speeds.Guinness World Records rules behind Peregreen 2's record-breaking drone speedA single high-speed run was not enough to establish the Guinness World Records achievement. The official rules required the drone to complete two successful flights in opposite directions. This method helps account for the effect of wind on the measured speed. A drone flying with a tailwind could record a higher ground speed, while a headwind could reduce the figure. Taking measurements in both directions allows the results to be assessed without giving either flight an advantage from prevailing wind conditions.Reportedly, Peregreen 2 completed the required runs, producing an average speed of 480.23 km/h. Its highest measured reading during the attempts was 510 km/h, but the average across the two flights was the figure used for the official record.The achievement was recognised under the specific category of fastest ground speed by a battery-powered remote-controlled quadcopter, distinguishing it from records involving other types of drones or aircraft.Mike and Luke Bell bring different experience to the projectMike Bell worked as an architect during his career and was involved in the design of Mbombela Stadium in South Africa. The stadium was one of the venues used during the 2010 FIFA World Cup, hosting four matches of the tournament. Luke, meanwhile, works as a content creator, producing material about drones and cameras for his YouTube and Instagram audiences. He is also an ambassador for Sony. His familiarity with camera equipment and drones provided a different perspective on the project, while his father's architectural background brought experience in design and construction.Peregreen 2 brought those interests together in a project that required both practical engineering and repeated experimentation. The record was not achieved in a single test session. It followed months of adjustments, including a complete redesign after the earlier Peregreen model failed to secure official recognition. By the time the second aircraft completed its record attempts, the team had produced a quadcopter capable of reaching speeds rarely associated with battery-powered remote-controlled machines.Disclaimer: This article is based on information published by Guinness World Records and other publicly available sources. The Times of India has not independently verified the technical details of the drone's construction or the record-setting attempts.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Norway has sent London a Christmas tree every year since 1947 to thank Britain for its wartime support; this year’s 75-year-old, 21-metre spruce has been named Jolly Cheery
articles.summary: A longstanding gesture of friendship between Norway and Britain is making its annual journey to London, as a 75-year-old Norwegian spruce has been felled
articles.body: A longstanding gesture of friendship between Norway and Britain is making its annual journey to London, as a 75-year-old Norwegian spruce has been felled for display at Trafalgar Square this Christmas. Named Jolly Cheery, the 21-metre tree was cut down in a forest outside Oslo on November 20, marking the beginning of its journey to the British capital, according to Westminster City Council, the City of Oslo and BBC News. The tree was felled by Westminster’s Lord Mayor Karen Scarborough and Oslo Mayor Anne Lindboe during a ceremony attended by schoolchildren who performed traditional Norwegian Christmas carols. The spruce, which grew in the Sørkedalen area of Oslo, was selected from three shortlisted candidates after members of the public were invited to express their preferences through social media.The annual gift carries a history that stretches back to the aftermath of the Second World War. Norway began sending a Christmas tree to London in 1947 as a gesture of gratitude for Britain’s support during the conflict. Following Germany’s occupation of Norway in 1940, King Haakon VII and the Norwegian government established themselves in exile in London, where they remained until the country’s liberation in 1945. What began as a gesture of appreciation has since developed into a symbol of the enduring relationship between the two countries. The tradition is now in its 79th year and has continued without interruption, with Oslo selecting a tree from its surrounding forests each November.Jolly Cheery will also make its journey to London using a transport arrangement designed to reduce its environmental impact. According to Westminster City Council, its road transportation in Norway and England will rely on electric and biodiesel-powered vehicles, reducing the journey’s carbon footprint by approximately 80 per cent. From Oslo, the tree will travel to the Norwegian port of Brevik before crossing the North Sea aboard a regular cargo vessel. It will then continue by road to London, where a specialist team will prepare it for installation in Trafalgar Square.Once erected, the spruce will be decorated in the traditional Norwegian style, with vertical strings of festoon lighting. The installation will feature 25-metre strings of lights fitted with energy-efficient bulbs, maintaining the distinctive appearance associated with the annual Christmas display. The lights are scheduled to be switched on by Scarborough and Lindboe at a public ceremony on Thursday, December 3, at 6 pm. The event traditionally marks the beginning of London’s Christmas celebrations, drawing visitors to one of the city’s best-known public squares.The tree’s selection process has also embraced public participation in recent years. For the second consecutive year, Oslo invited residents to choose their favourite from a shortlist shared on social media, with the mayor considering public feedback alongside expert recommendations before making the final selection.After the festive season, the tree will not simply be discarded. Following the tradition, it will be removed from Trafalgar Square and recycled into compost, giving the Norwegian spruce another purpose after its time as London’s Christmas centrepiece. Nearly eight decades after the first tree arrived from Norway, the annual tradition continues to connect two countries through a simple but meaningful gesture. This year’s Jolly Cheery will bring that familiar reminder of friendship, gratitude and shared history to the heart of London.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Delhi high court nixes order to cancel NGO’s FCRA licence
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Taking a dim view of the home ministry’s reluctance to share even with the court the inputs that led it to cancel the FCRA licence of an NGO
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Taking a dim view of the home ministry’s reluctance to share even with the court the inputs that led it to cancel the FCRA licence of an NGO engaged in legal aid, Delhi high court on Thursday set aside the decision. HC said the move to cancel the licence of NGO Socio Legal Information Centre (SLIC) based solely on the allegation that it has indulged in “aggressive anti-government political activism” was without any material.HC said no material was furnished by government to show that SLIC’s activities would likely prejudicially affect the sovereignty, integrity or security of India or the public interest.Delhi HC: No proof of ‘anti-government activism’ charge against NGOWhile government contends that the violations on the appellant’s NGO’s part were brought to its notice through ‘security inputs’, which cannot be divulged since they are ‘secret’; this court is of the view that such inputs cannot be kept secret to the point that no material is brought even to the notice of this court, though the appellant has faced the drastic action of having its FCRA registration cancelled, arising from such inputs,” Justice AJ Bhambhani of Delhi HC said.“The respondent’s (Centre) allegation that the appellant has indulged in ‘aggressive anti-government political activism’ is also not based on any material. No documents or other material has been placed on record by the respondent to support that allegation,” HC added in its judgement.It said unless something sinister comes through from material available against it, an organisation that is engaged in assisting aggrieved persons in raising their grievances before courts and statutory commissions, acting through the available constitutional machinery, cannot be characterised as engaging in “political activity” or in activities impinging on political and law-and-order domains. “In the impugned cancellation order, the respondent has also alleged that the appellant’s activities amount to an attempt to portray a ‘wrong image of public institutions of India in the eyes of international community’. This court would observe that this allegation strains credulity; and this court is dismayed by the respondent’s attempt to baselessly portray the appellant organisation in such light,” it said.HC’s verdict came on a plea by the NGO seeking to set aside the Oct 2022 order of the home ministry cancelling its Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act registration certificate. articles.title: Leopard hunt on in Kanpur, forest team combs 8km radius
articles.summary: Kanpur forest department searches for leopard after Karankheda attack, combing 6–8km with drones, trap cams and cages; villagers warned to stay alert.
articles.body: Kanpur: The forest department continued its search and rescue operation following a leopard attack in Karankheda village under Maharajpur police station in Kanpur, but the animal’s exact location remained unknown.A team comprising DFO Akanksha Jain, doctors, zoo rescuers and about 22 forest personnel conducted combing operations within a 6km-8km radius, covering fields and the Ganga Katri area. Cages, trap cameras, night-vision cameras, drones and tranquiliser guns were deployed to capture the leopard.Remains of livestock killed by an animal were found on Tuesday night, while paw marks of a wild animal were spotted about 200 metres from the site.The incident triggered panic among Karankheda’s nearly 30,000 residents and people in about 12 nearby villages.As the riverbank area adjoins a forest, wildlife could move towards populated areas.Jain advised villagers not to visit fields alone, to keep children safe and to travel in groups when necessary.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Kanpur | Silver Rate in Kanpur | Bank Holidays in Kanpur | Public Holidays in Kanpur | Kanpur AQI | Weather in Kanpur | Petrol Price in Kanpur | Diesel Price in Kanpur | CNG Price in Kanpur | LPG Price in KanpurStay updated with the latest Kanpur news. articles.title: CIA's secret torture programme: New files reveal more accounts of waterboarding claims than agency admitted
articles.summary: The CIA may have waterboarded more terrorism suspects than the three detainees it has officially acknowledged subjecting to the torture technique after
articles.body: The CIA may have waterboarded more terrorism suspects than the three detainees it has officially acknowledged subjecting to the torture technique after the September 11, 2001, attacks, a New York Times report has revealed. The disclosure comes from newly declassified records released by the US government following a newspaper lawsuit under the Freedom of Information Act. The records include a former CIA contractor's account of witnessing a waterboarding session at a secret detention facility in Afghanistan.The former contract translator, who worked at a CIA black site, told an FBI agent in 2012 that he had seen a detainee identified as “Bahir” strapped to a board and tilted downwards into water. The account suggests that the agency may have used waterboarding at its Afghanistan facility, an instance not included in its official count.According to an FBI agent's summary of the interview, the translator said: “There were approximately three to four people ‘doing this’.” The agent added that the witness “saw the incident in passing but did not participate himself. The waterboard session was in the hallway and there was not a lot of room.”The newly released material does not establish how many detainees were waterboarded at the facility or conclusively identify the man described by the translator.What CIA officially admittedThe CIA had told the Senate Intelligence Committee that its records showed only three detainees had been waterboarded as part of its post-9/11 interrogation programme.They were Abu Zubaydah, the first detainee held in the agency's secret prison network; Khalid Shaikh Mohammed, accused of masterminding the September 11 attacks; and Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri, accused of helping plan the 2000 bombing of the USS Cole.All three are currently held at the US military prison at Guantanamo Bay. They were waterboarded at CIA black sites in Thailand and Poland, not at the Afghanistan facility.The former translator's account raises fresh questions about whether the agency's records gave a complete picture of its use of the technique.Earlier allegations of waterboarding in AfghanistanThere have been previous indications that the CIA may have used waterboarding at its secret detention facility north of Kabul, known as the Salt Pit or Detention Site Cobalt.In 2012, a Libyan man previously held at the facility told Human Rights Watch that he had been waterboarded there. However, the Senate Intelligence Committee's 2014 report did not mention the technique in its account of his detention.The report said CIA records showed that the man had been subjected to other interrogation methods, including confinement in a cramped box and painful stress positions. It also acknowledged that detainees at the facility had been subjected to techniques “not recorded in cable traffic”.A footnote in the report revealed that investigators had obtained a photograph of a waterboard at the Afghanistan facility, surrounded by buckets of liquid. When committee staff questioned the CIA about the photograph in 2013, the agency was “unable to explain”.The newly released interview report also refers to “Bahir”, whom the translator described as “a relative of Hekmatyar”. This appears to be a reference to a prominent Afghan militia leader and politician from the 1980s and 1990s.The Senate report lists a detainee named Ghairat Bahir, whom CIA records show was held for about two years from 2002 and subjected to what the agency called “enhanced” interrogation techniques. However, it remains unclear whether he was the man described by the translator.Records linked to investigation into CIA tortureThe documents were part of former special prosecutor John Durham's investigation into the CIA's use of torture and the destruction of videotapes showing waterboarding sessions. The investigation ran from 2008 to 2012 but did not result in criminal charges against agency personnel.The government has continued to withhold Durham's reports on his findings.The Senate Intelligence Committee conducted a parallel investigation and released a more than 500-page executive summary in 2014. Its inquiry relied largely on millions of pages of internal CIA records because agency witnesses were unwilling to be interviewed while Durham's criminal investigation was under way.The CIA press office did not respond to a request for comment on the newly released material.CIA officials feared tapes could 'destroy a president'Other interview reports released this week shed light on the agency's concerns over videotapes of detainee interrogations and the possibility that they could become public.One official told the FBI that he had kept the tapes in a safe, describing them as “serious business”. He also expressed concern “that if the tapes got into the wrong hands they could have the potential to ‘destroy a president.’”The records indicate that CIA officials feared the videos could be made public after George W. Bush left office and that agency personnel could face prosecution.In an interview on January 22, 2009, two days after Barack Obama took office, one official recalled that the CIA had earlier raised concerns with Bush's chief of staff, Andrew H. Card, about the possibility of prosecutions linked to the tapes.According to the official, Card conveyed the concerns to Bush and later said the president had responded that “there was only one person he could not pardon, and that was himself, implying the president would take executive action should any CIA employees find themselves being prosecuted for their work on the interrogation program.”The newly released accounts also include interviews concerning Abu Zubaydah. Former FBI agent Ali Soufan, who helped question Zubaydah and opposed the CIA's use of torture, said the accounts matched his recollection.
